etymology: From the Old English thider, “to that place,” formed on the same demonstrative stem as that and there; hence motion toward a place away from the speaker — the answer to whither, as there answers where.
biblical_def: Thither is the old adverb of motion toward — not there, which marks rest in a place, but thither, which marks the going to it. The KJV keeps the distinction our speech has lost, and the loss is not small, for Scripture is full of men on the way to somewhere. The manslayer has a thither: the LORD appointed cities of refuge “that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11) — a place named beforehand, a road prepared, a gate that stands open to the pursued. So Christ is the refuge to which the guilty run. Moses had a thither he was not given: the LORD showed him the land from Nebo and said, “thou shalt not go over thither” (Deu 34:4) — the servant sees the promise and the greater Joshua brings the people in. The word governs the doctrine of the effectual Word: as the rain “returneth not thither, but watereth the earth” (Isa 55:10), so God’s word does not go out and come back empty but accomplishes that which He pleases. And it falls with terrible weight from the lips of Christ upon the unbelieving: “where I am, thither ye cannot come” (Joh 7:34). There is a place whither the Lord is gone and a road thither, and the man who will not come by Him shall seek and not find. Every soul is travelling somewhere. The only question the word asks is whether the thither is the refuge or the dark.
webster_summary: To that place; toward that place — the adverb of motion toward, answering to whither.
webster_full: THITHER, to that place; used of motion toward, not of rest in.
From the Saxon thider, of the same stem as that and there.
It answers to whither, as there answers to where.
The slayer fled thither, to the appointed city of refuge (Num 35:11).
Christ says of Himself, “where I am, thither ye cannot come” (Joh 7:34).
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Deu 34:4

And the LORD said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither.

For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:
Joh 7:34
Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word of motion toward; it recovers that every soul is travelling somewhere, and that the refuge has a road to it.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age with no thither. Modern speech has collapsed whither and thither into a flat where, and the flattening of the grammar has followed the flattening of the life: men move endlessly and arrive nowhere, calling the motion itself the meaning. Scripture will not have it. The manslayer ran to a named city on a cleared road; Israel marched toward a sworn land; the rain falls and does not return thither empty. Motion in the Bible has a terminus, appointed by God before the runner ever set out.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there are only two destinations, and Christ is the road to the one worth reaching. The LORD appointed cities of refuge that the slayer might flee thither and live — and the gospel appoints a refuge for men who have shed blood far worse, with the gate standing open and the avenger behind. But there is also the word of Joh 7:34: “where I am, thither ye cannot come.” The Lord has gone to the Father, and the man who refuses the only way shall seek Him and not find Him. Let a man ask not whether he is moving but whither, and by what road.
roots_summary: The word means “to that place” — motion toward, as distinct from rest in a place.
roots_lines: Thither — Old English thider, “to that place.”
Built on the demonstrative stem of that and there.
It marks motion toward; there marks rest in the place.
It is the answer to the question whither, “to what place?”
The slayer fled thither to the city of refuge and lived (Num 35:11).
usage: The slayer fled thither: God named the refuge and cleared the road before ever the blood was shed.
Moses saw the land but might not go over thither — the servant sees; the greater Joshua brings in.
The rain returneth not thither empty, and neither does the word that goeth out of God’s mouth.

etymology: From the Old English hider, “to this place,” formed on the same demonstrative stem as he and here; the near counterpart of thither — motion toward the speaker, as here is rest with the speaker.
biblical_def: Hither is the adverb of motion toward the speaker — come hither, to this place, to me. It is the summoning word of Scripture, and it is almost always God who speaks it. Joseph, at the great reconciliation, lays his whole story at the feet of providence: “it was not you that sent me hither, but God” (Gen 45:8). The brothers meant a pit and a caravan; the LORD meant a throne in Egypt and bread for a famished house. Every hither in a saint’s life has a hand behind it that is not his own. Yet the word can also fence: from the burning bush the LORD cries, “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exo 3:5). God summons, and God also sets a bound; the same voice that calls a man near tells him how near, and on what terms, a creature may approach the Holy One. In the risen Christ the bound is graciously crossed: “Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands… and be not faithless, but believing” (Joh 20:27). The Lord bids the doubter come and touch the very wounds. And the last hither is the sweetest of all — a trumpet-voice from an opened door in heaven saying, “Come up hither” (Rev 4:1). Moses is fenced out, Thomas is called in, John is called up. The whole Christian life lies between the Draw not nigh hither of Sinai and the Come up hither of glory, and Christ is the difference.
webster_summary: To this place; toward the speaker — the near adverb of motion, answering to thither.
webster_full: HITHER, to this place; used of motion toward the speaker.
From the Saxon hider, of the same stem as here.
It is the near counterpart of thither, which points away.
It is the summoning word — “come hither,” “bring hither,” “reach hither.”
At the bush the LORD said, “Draw not nigh hither” (Exo 3:5).
scriptures: Gen 45:8
So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God: and he hath made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house, and a ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.
Exo 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
Rev 4:1

After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word of nearness; it recovers that God both summons the sinner hither and sets the bound on how a creature may approach.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that assumes an easy access. Men speak of coming to God as though the door were their own and the terms theirs to set, forgetting that the first hither in the Bible is a prohibition: “Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet.” The bush burned and was not consumed, and Moses hid his face. God is not approachable on the sinner’s terms, at the sinner’s hour, in the sinner’s shoes. Where reverence dies, the sense of holy ground dies with it, and the God who is a consuming fire is remade into a companion who never fences anything.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God summons, and Christ makes the summons safe. Joseph knew it was God, not his brothers, that sent him hither — every step of a saint’s road is drawn by a hand he cannot see. The risen Lord said to a doubter, “Reach hither thy finger,” and bade him touch the wounds that bought him. And from an open door in heaven the trumpet says, “Come up hither.” Sinai fences the creature out; Calvary calls him in; glory calls him up. Between the two hithers stands the blood, and there is no other way near.
roots_summary: The word means “to this place” — motion toward the speaker, the near counterpart of thither.
roots_lines: Hither — Old English hider, “to this place.”
Built on the near demonstrative stem that also gives here.
It marks motion toward the speaker; thither points away.
It is the word of summons — come, bring, reach, draw hither.
It is also the word of bound: “Draw not nigh hither” (Exo 3:5).
usage: It was not you that sent me hither, but God — Joseph reads a pit and a caravan as providence.
Draw not nigh hither: the God who calls a man near also tells him how near, and on what terms.
Reach hither thy finger — the risen Christ bids the doubter touch the wounds that bought him.

etymology: A running-together of the three words for as much (as), an English rendering of the Latin quoniam and the Greek epeidēper; hence “seeing that, in consideration that, because” — the conjunction that lays down a ground before it draws a conclusion.
biblical_def: Forasmuch is the conjunction of grounded reasoning: seeing that, in consideration that, because. It never stands alone. It reaches back to a settled fact and forward to what must follow from it, and Scripture uses it as the hinge on which the great arguments turn. Luke opens his Gospel with it (Luk 1:1) — the evangelist writes because the facts are already most surely believed, not to make them so. Peter grounds a whole life of holy fear in it: “Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold” (1Pe 1:18) — the redeemed live thus because they were bought thus. And Hebrews hangs the incarnation on it: “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same” (Heb 2:14). The Son took our nature because His children had it, and He took it to destroy death by dying. In the mouth of the LORD the word can also indict: “Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth… but have removed their heart far from me” (Isa 29:13) — the ground is named, and the judgment follows. Here is the shape of all biblical religion. The indicative comes first and the imperative after; what God has done is the reason for what we must do. Strike out the forasmuch and the commands become mere moralism, floating free of the cross that grounds them.
webster_summary: Seeing that; in consideration that; because — the conjunction that lays down a ground before drawing a conclusion.
webster_full: FORASMUCH, in consideration that; seeing that; since; because.
A compound of for, as, and much, run together into one word.
It renders the Latin quoniam and the Greek epeidēper.
It states the ground on which the following conclusion rests.
Luke writes his Gospel “forasmuch as many have taken in hand” (Luk 1:1).
scriptures: Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
Luk 1:1
Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us,
Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the plain conjunction of grounded reasoning; it recovers that the indicative comes first and the imperative after — commands rest on the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a religion of bare imperatives. Isaiah’s people drew near with the mouth and honoured with the lips, and their fear toward God was “taught by the precept of men” — duty learned by rote, with no living ground beneath it. That is moralism, and it is the oldest counterfeit there is: the outward form of obedience with the heart removed far away. A pulpit that preaches only what men must do, and never the forasmuch of what God has done, breeds either the proud who think they have kept it or the crushed who know they have not. Both are strangers to grace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the gospel. Peter does not say, Be holy, and perhaps you shall be redeemed; he says, Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things — therefore pass the time of your sojourning in fear. Hebrews does not speculate why the Son took flesh; it says, Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, He likewise took part of the same. The finished work grounds the command; the command never props up the work. Every duty a Christian owes hangs on a forasmuch, and every forasmuch hangs on the blood of Christ.
roots_summary: The word means “seeing that, because” — a ground stated before a conclusion is drawn.
roots_lines: Forasmuch — a running-together of for as much (as).
It renders Latin quoniam and Greek epeidēper, “since, because.”
It states a settled ground and draws a conclusion from it.
It marks the gospel order: the indicative first, the imperative after.
Redemption is its greatest ground — forasmuch as ye were bought (1Pe 1:18).
usage: Forasmuch as ye were not redeemed with silver and gold: the ransom is the reason for the holy life.
Forasmuch as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, the Son took the same — and died.
Strike out the forasmuch and the commandments float free of the cross that grounds them.

etymology: A compound of with and all, standing where modern English would say therewith or besides; in the KJV it serves two turns — the instrumental (that with which a thing is done) and the additive (moreover, at the same time).
biblical_def: Withal is a small word doing two large offices. Most often it is instrumental — it names the means, the thing with which a work is done, standing at the end of the clause where our speech would put therewith. The LORD commands a laver of brass “to wash withal” (Exo 30:18), set between the tent and the altar: the priest may not serve until he is washed, and God provides the very vessel. Christ uses it of the measure a man carries: “with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again” (Luk 6:38) — the grudging cup you weigh with is the cup that shall be weighed back to you, and the liberal hand is met with good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over. Paul uses it of the Spirit’s gifts: the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man “to profit withal” (1Co 12:7). Not one gift is given for the man who has it; every gift is a tool put into his hand for the profit of the body. The other office is additive: “Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance” (Col 4:3) — moreover, along with all the rest, pray. So the word teaches the doctrine of means. God does not merely command the end; He appoints the laver, the measure, the gift, the prayer, and hands them to us with the command. The Christian is never told to work without being told what to work withal.
webster_summary: With it; therewith; along with the rest; moreover, at the same time.
webster_full: WITHAL, with it; with them; therewith; used at the close of a clause.
A compound of with and all, standing for the modern therewith.
In one sense instrumental — the thing with which a work is done.
In another sense additive — moreover, besides, at the same time.
The laver was made to wash withal; the gifts are given to profit withal.
scriptures: Thou shalt also make a laver of brass, and his foot also of brass, to wash withal: and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein.
Luk 6:38

Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
Col 4:3
Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds:
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for the means; it recovers that God appoints not only the end He commands but the instrument He commands it withal.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes two errors at once. The first is the man who claims a gift and keeps it: the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal — a tool for the body, not an ornament for the owner. Gifts hoarded are gifts abused. The second is the man who measures out to others with a stingy cup and expects a generous one in return; but with the same measure that ye mete withal, it shall be measured to you again. The instrument in a man’s hand tells the truth about his heart, and it is the instrument God notices.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of means. God never commands an end and leaves us to invent the way to it: He set a laver of brass between the tent and the altar, filled it with water, and said, wash withal. He gives the Spirit’s gifts and says, profit withal. He commands the door of utterance to be opened and says, withal pray. The Lord who ordains the harvest ordains the plough, and the Christian who despises the appointed means while claiming to seek the appointed end is not trusting God but tempting Him. Use the laver He gave you to wash withal.
roots_summary: The word means “with it, therewith” — and also “moreover, besides.”
roots_lines: Withal — a compound of with and all.
It stands where modern English says therewith or besides.
In the instrumental sense it names the means of a work (Exo 30:18).
In the additive sense it means moreover, at the same time (Col 4:3).
The gifts of the Spirit are given to every man to profit withal (1Co 12:7).
usage: The laver was set between tent and altar, to wash withal — God gives the vessel with the command.
With the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again — mind your cup.
Every gift is given to profit withal: a tool for the body, never an ornament for the owner.

etymology: From strait (Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow”) + -ly; hence strictly, closely, urgently, with binding force. It has no kinship with straight, “not crooked” — a strait is a narrow place, and to charge straitly is to bind narrowly.
biblical_def: Straitly means strictly, closely, with a binding tightness — the adverb of a charge that leaves no room to move. It is not our word straight; a strait is a narrow passage, and to be straitly charged is to be hemmed in by the command. Joseph “straitly sworn” his brethren about his bones (Exo 13:19), and four hundred years later Moses carried them out of Egypt: an oath bound that tight outlives the man who took it. Jericho “was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel: none went out, and none came in” (Jos 6:1) — a city sealed as tight as fear could seal it, and the walls fell anyway at the appointed shout. Our Lord uses the word constantly in Mark: cleansing the leper, “he straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away” (Mar 1:43); and so with the healed blind, and the devils, and the raised child. Christ is no seeker of crowds; He binds men to silence, refusing a fame built on wonders rather than on the cross. The word turns dark in Acts, where the council flings it back at the apostles: “Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name?” (Act 5:28). Here two straitly-charges meet head-on — the Sanhedrin’s and Christ’s — and Peter answers that we ought to obey God rather than men. Every man is straitly charged by someone. The only question is whose narrow command binds him when the two commands cross.
webster_summary: Strictly; closely; urgently; with binding force — from strait, narrow, not from straight.
webster_full: STRAITLY, strictly; rigorously; with a close and binding charge.
From strait, Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow”; not from straight.
Also closely, narrowly, as a city straitly shut up (Jos 6:1).
Joseph straitly sware the children of Israel concerning his bones (Exo 13:19).
Christ straitly charged the healed to tell no man (Mar 1:43).
scriptures: And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you.
Jos 6:1
Now Jericho was straitly shut up because of the children of Israel: none went out, and none came in.
Mar 1:43
And he straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away;
Act 5:28
Saying, Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name? and, behold, ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us.
corruption_summary: A live misuse, and a plain one: the age will be straitly charged by nothing, having reduced God’s binding commands to suggestions and His narrow way to a matter of taste.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a real corruption here, and it is not of the word but of the thing. Our generation recognizes no straitly. Commands are heard as preferences, vows as intentions, and the moral law as counsel a man may weigh against his feelings. Joseph straitly sware his brethren, and the oath held its grip on a nation for four hundred years until Moses hoisted the coffin and marched. Christ straitly charged the men He healed, and the charge bound them. But an easy-believism that will confess a Saviour and refuse a Lord has emptied the adverb out of religion altogether: it wants the healing without the charge, the benefit without the binding, and a God whose every word may be renegotiated. A command that binds nothing has commanded nothing.

Two straitly-charges meet in Acts, and every believer will one day stand where they cross. The council said, “Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name?” — and Christ had straitly commanded the very opposite, that repentance and remission be preached in His name among all nations. Peter did not split the difference or seek the middle: we ought to obey God rather than men. The world will always have a straitly of its own, and it grows bolder as the church grows softer. Note also that Jericho was straitly shut up, none going out and none coming in — and the walls fell flat at the appointed shout. No strictness of man can bind what God has purposed to open.
roots_summary: The word means strictly, closely, with binding force — from strait, narrow.
roots_lines: Straitly — from strait, Latin strictus, “drawn tight, narrow.”
It is no kin to straight; a strait is a narrow place, not an unbent line.
It denotes a charge so close that it leaves no room to move.
Jericho was straitly shut up, and the walls fell anyway (Jos 6:1).
The council straitly commanded silence; Christ straitly commanded preaching.
usage: Joseph straitly sware his brethren, and the oath held a nation four hundred years (Exo 13:19).
Christ straitly charged the healed leper — He would not build a fame on wonders instead of the cross.
The council straitly commanded silence; Peter answered that we ought to obey God rather than men.

etymology: A compound of afore (Old English onforan, “before, in front of”) and time; hence formerly, in time past, in former days — that which was done or written before the present hour.
biblical_def: Aforetime means formerly, in time past — and the word is never a mere date. It carries the weight of what went before into what is now. Isaiah recalls a nation’s history to steady it in its present distress: “My people went down aforetime into Egypt to sojourn there; and the Assyrian oppressed them without cause” (Isa 52:4). The God who brought them out of the one house of bondage will bring them out of the other; the past is the pledge. In Daniel the word measures a man’s spine: when the writing was signed and the lions’ den was law, Daniel went home, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and kneeled three times a day “as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10). He did not add a prayer for the crisis nor subtract one for the danger — he did what he had always done. That is what habit is for: the settled practice of ordinary days is the only thing that stands up on the day the decree is signed. John names a healed man simply as him “that aforetime was blind” (Joh 9:13) — a whole biography in one adverb, the old life named and left. And Paul makes the word a doctrine of Scripture: “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope” (Rom 15:4). The Old Testament is not an archive but a schoolroom. What was written aforetime was written for us, and hope is the thing it teaches.
webster_summary: In time past; formerly; in former days — that which was done or written before the present hour.
webster_full: AFORETIME, in time past; in a former time; formerly.
A compound of afore, “before,” and time.
Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem as he did aforetime (Dan 6:10).
The healed man is named him that aforetime was blind (Joh 9:13).
Whatsoever was written aforetime was written for our learning (Rom 15:4).
scriptures: Isa 52:4
For thus saith the Lord GOD, My people went down aforetime into Egypt to sojourn there; and the Assyrian oppressed them without cause.
Dan 6:10

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
Joh 9:13
They brought to the Pharisees him that aforetime was blind.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
corruption_summary: A live misuse: the age despises what was written aforetime as merely ancient, and so throws away the schoolroom God gave His church for hope.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption worth naming. Our generation holds a settled contempt for the past — the assumption that what is older is thereby outgrown, that the fathers were simply mistaken about what we have lately discovered, and that a text written aforetime can bind no one now. The academy dresses this up as method, treating the Old Testament as the fossil of a religion rather than the word of the living God; the church absorbs the mood without the argument and quietly stops reading it. Paul says the opposite in one flat sentence: whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning. Not for the archivist. For us. And the fruit of that learning is not information but hope.

The remedy Daniel shows is habit. When the writing was signed and prayer was made a capital crime, he went home, opened the windows toward Jerusalem, and kneeled three times a day “as he did aforetime” — changing nothing, because there was nothing to change. Courage on the day of the decree is only the overflow of obedience on the thousand days before it. The man who prays only in crisis will not pray in the lions’ den. So too the healed man of John 9, named forever as him that aforetime was blind: the past is not erased by grace but transfigured by it, kept as the dark backdrop against which the mercy shows. Despise the aforetime and you lose the learning, the hope, the habit, and the testimony together.
roots_summary: The word means formerly, in time past — what was done or written before the present hour.
roots_lines: Aforetime — a compound of afore and time.
From Old English onforan, “before, in front of.”
It denotes former days, the settled past behind the present hour.
Daniel kneeled and prayed as he did aforetime, decree or no decree (Dan 6:10).
What was written aforetime was written for our learning and hope (Rom 15:4).
usage: Daniel prayed as he did aforetime: the habit of ordinary days is what stands on the day of the decree.
Whatsoever was written aforetime was written for our learning — the Old Testament is a schoolroom.
He that aforetime was blind: grace does not erase the old life, it makes the mercy visible against it.

etymology: From the Old English wiht, “a thing, a creature, a bit” (the same word that gives wight and the -whit of naught); hence the smallest particle, the least conceivable part — chiefly in the phrases every whit (the whole, without exception) and not a whit (not in the least).
biblical_def: A whit is the least particle, the smallest imaginable part — and the KJV uses it almost always to say all of something, or none. When the LORD gave the boy Samuel a terrible word against the house of Eli, “Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him” (1Sa 3:18): not the softened sum of the message but the whole of it, down to the last bit. That is the standard for every man who handles God’s word — declare the whole counsel and keep back nothing, though the hearer be your master and the message be his ruin. The word’s glory, though, is in the mouth of Christ, where it measures His work. To the men angry at a sabbath healing He answers, “are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day?” (Joh 7:23). Not mended, not improved, not partly restored — every whit whole. And in the upper room He says of the washed disciple that he “is clean every whit” (Joh 13:10), needing only his feet washed for the day’s dust; the great washing is done once and is complete. Here is justification and sanctification distinguished in a single sentence. Paul turns the word the other way: “I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles” (2Co 11:5) — not by the least particle. So the whit is the enemy of every half-measure. Christ heals every whit, cleanses every whit, and His servants must speak every whit and keep back not a whit.
webster_summary: The smallest particle; a bit; the least conceivable part — chiefly in every whit, the whole, and not a whit, not at all.
webster_full: WHIT, a point; a jot; the smallest part or particle imaginable.
From the Saxon wiht, “a thing, a creature, a bit.”
In every whit it means the whole, down to the last part.
In not a whit it means not in the least degree (2Co 11:5).
Christ made the man every whit whole, and the washed are clean every whit.
scriptures: And Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him. And he said, It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.
Joh 7:23
If a man on the sabbath day receive circumcision, that the law of Moses should not be broken; are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day?
Jesus saith to him, He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all.
For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for the least particle; it recovers that Christ saves every whit and that His preachers must keep back not a whit.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the preacher who trims. Samuel was a boy with a crushing word against the man who raised him, and he told him every whit, and hid nothing from him. The temptation of every pulpit is to keep back a whit — the hard doctrine, the naming of a sin the hearers love, the wrath of God, the narrowness of the way — and to call the keeping-back kindness. It is not kindness. A message with a whit held back is a different message, and the man who hears it has not heard from God. Declare the whole counsel and let the LORD do what seemeth Him good.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ’s work is entire. He did not make the man mostly whole but every whit whole; He does not leave the washed disciple partly clean but clean every whit, needing only the feet washed of the day’s dust. There is the whole Reformed doctrine in a phrase: the great bathing is done once, complete, unrepeatable — that is justification; the daily washing of the feet is the ongoing cleansing of the pilgrim — that is sanctification. Any gospel that leaves the sinner to supply the missing whit has denied the finished work. What Christ washes is clean every whit, or He is no Saviour at all.
roots_summary: The word means the smallest particle, the least conceivable part of a thing.
roots_lines: Whit — Old English wiht, “a thing, a creature, a bit.”
It is kin to wight and to the -ght of naught, “no whit.”
It denotes the least particle, a jot, the smallest part imaginable.
Every whit means the whole, without exception (Joh 13:10).
Not a whit means not in the least degree (2Co 11:5).
usage: Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing — the preacher who trims a whit preaches another word.
Christ made the man every whit whole: no half-healing ever left the Saviour’s hand.
He that is washed is clean every whit, and needs but his feet washed of the day’s dust.

etymology: From the Middle English at do, a northern form of “to do” borrowed from the Norse construction; hence bustle, stir, tumult, trouble — a great deal of doing, and commonly a great deal of noise about it.
biblical_def: Ado is bustle, stir, tumult — the noise men make about a thing. It occurs but once in all Scripture, and it falls from the lips of Christ in the house of a dead child. Jairus’s daughter lay lifeless, and the Lord “seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly” (Mar 5:38) — the hired mourners of the East, whose grief was a trade and whose wailing was engaged by the hour. Into that hubbub He walks and asks, “Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth” (Mar 5:39). The question is not cruelty but authority. He who was about to call the girl by the hand out of death saw the professional grief for what it was: loud, sincere-sounding, and utterly ignorant of what was standing in the room. And the mourners answered as such a crowd always answers — “they laughed him to scorn” (Mar 5:40). The same mouths that wailed a moment before could laugh in an instant; the emotion was on a tap. So Christ put them all out. He raised the child with none present but the parents and three disciples, in a room emptied of the ado. The lesson is plain and searching. God is not moved by volume. Ecclesiastes says it flatly: “God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few” (Ecc 5:2). Where Christ works, the noise goes out first.
webster_summary: Bustle; stir; tumult; trouble — a great deal of doing, and commonly a great deal of noise about it.
webster_full: ADO, bustle; trouble; tumult; business with difficulty and noise.
From the Middle English at do, a northern form of “to do.”
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Mar 5:39).
It names the wailing of the hired mourners in the ruler’s house.
Christ put the ado out of doors before He raised the child (Mar 5:40).
scriptures: Mar 5:38
And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly.
Mar 5:39
And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth.
Mar 5:40
And they laughed him to scorn. But when he had put them all out, he taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entereth in where the damsel was lying.
Ecc 5:2
Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.
corruption_summary: A live misuse, and one the modern church has industrialized: the ado of manufactured religious feeling, mistaken for the presence and power of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption to name honestly. The hired mourners of Mark 5 wept and wailed greatly for a fee, and their grief was real enough to be loud and false enough to turn to laughter in a breath. The modern parallel is not hard to find. A great deal of what passes for the power of God is ado — engineered feeling, the swell of the music timed to the swell of the appeal, the manufactured hush and the manufactured shout, the tears counted as evidence. This is the working principle of every revivalist technique from the anxious bench onward: produce the emotion and call it the Spirit. But feeling that a stage can generate, a stage can also dismiss, and the crowd that wails on cue will laugh Christ to scorn on cue. God is in heaven and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few.

Notice what our Lord actually did: “he put them all out.” The room where the dead was raised had no ado in it — only the father, the mother, three disciples, and the Christ who takes a corpse by the hand and speaks. The regulative principle of worship is this same instinct written into the church’s order: we bring what God has commanded and leave outside what He has not, precisely so that the ado of man cannot be mistaken for the work of God. Real grief is holy and Christ never mocked it — He wept at a grave Himself. What He put out was the trade in grief, the noise that is about the mourners rather than the dead. Where He works, He works in a quiet room, and the girl arose.
roots_summary: The word means bustle, stir, tumult — much doing, and much noise about it.
roots_lines: Ado — from Middle English at do, a northern “to do.”
It denotes bustle, stir, trouble, tumult, business made loud.
A KJV hapax, spoken once, by Christ, in a house of death (Mar 5:39).
It names the wailing trade of the hired mourners of the East.
Christ put the ado out of doors, then raised the child (Mar 5:40).
usage: Why make ye this ado? The hired mourners wailed by the hour and knew nothing of who had come in.
They laughed him to scorn: grief that can be turned on by a trade can be turned off by a jest.
He put them all out — where Christ raises the dead, the ado goes out of doors first.

etymology: From the Old English behōfian, “to have need of, to be fitting or necessary,” from behōf, “need, advantage, behoof”; hence it must, it was needful, it was fitting. The KJV spells it behoved; the modern form doubles the o.
biblical_def: To behoove is to be needful, fitting, and necessary — and in the KJV the word is reserved almost wholly for the sufferings of Christ. It is the divine must. On the road to Emmaus and again in the upper room the risen Lord opens the Scriptures and says, “Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day” (Luk 24:46). Note what the necessity rests on: thus it is written. The cross was no accident of Roman politics or Jewish envy; it was the eternal counsel of God, published beforehand in Moses and the prophets, and it behoved the Christ to walk into it. He had already pressed the same question on the two: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luk 24:26). Paul preaches nothing else at Thessalonica, alleging “that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead” (Act 17:3). And Hebrews tells us why the necessity reached even to His nature: “in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest… to make reconciliation for the sins of the people” (Heb 2:17). He must be man to die for men; He must die to satisfy justice; He must rise to justify the dead in Adam. Nothing here is arbitrary. Given a holy God, a broken law, and a people given to the Son before the world was, it behoved Him — and He came.
webster_summary: It was needful, fitting, or necessary; it must be — used in the KJV chiefly of the divine necessity of Christ’s sufferings.
webster_full: BEHOVE (behoove), to be necessary, fit, or meet for; to be needful.
From the Saxon behōfian, “to need,” from behōf, “need, behoof.”
In Scripture it is impersonal — it behoved — and marks necessity, not mere fitness.
Thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise the third day (Luk 24:46).
In all things it behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren (Heb 2:17).
scriptures: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?
And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:
Act 17:3
Opening and alleging, that Christ must needs have suffered, and risen again from the dead; and that this Jesus, whom I preach unto you, is Christ.
Heb 2:17

Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
corruption_summary: The plain old word for a divine must; it recovers that the cross was not a tragedy God made the best of but the necessity He purposed before the world was.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes every attempt to make the cross optional. The moral-influence theory, revived and popularized in our own day, will have Calvary as a demonstration of love and nothing more — a moving example, not a satisfaction; and the progressive evangelical objection that a Father who requires the death of His Son is guilty of cruelty (Steve Chalke’s formulation is the best-known) strikes at the same nerve. But the risen Christ did not say it was beautiful that He should suffer; He said it behoved Him to suffer, and grounded the must in what was written. Take away the necessity and the atonement collapses into theatre — a God performing love at a bloody cost He did not actually need to pay. Scripture knows no such God. Justice must be satisfied or the Judge of all the earth does not do right.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the divine must is a mercy. It behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren — flesh, blood, hunger, weariness, temptation, death — that He might be a merciful and faithful high priest and make reconciliation for the sins of the people. He did not have to save; He was under no compulsion but His own eternal purpose, and the covenant of redemption laid the necessity on Him because He had freely undertaken it. That is why the must is good news. Given a holy God, a broken law, and a people given to the Son before the foundation of the world, the way to the throne ran through Golgotha and He would not turn aside. It behoved Him — and He came.
roots_summary: The word means it was needful, fitting, necessary — the divine must of Christ’s work.
roots_lines: Behoove — Old English behōfian, “to have need of.”
From behōf, “need, advantage, behoof”; the KJV spells it behoved.
It is impersonal — it behoved — and states a necessity, not a preference.
It behoved Christ to suffer and to rise the third day, for thus it is written.
It behoved Him to be made like His brethren, to be a merciful high priest.
usage: Thus it behoved Christ to suffer: the cross was written before it was hammered.
It behoved Him to be made like unto His brethren — He must be man to die for men.
The divine must is no compulsion upon God but the freely-undertaken covenant of redemption.

etymology: From the Old English lēof, “dear, beloved, pleasing” — the same root that gives love and the -lief of belief. As an adjective it means dear; as the adverb of the old phrase I had as lief, it means gladly, willingly, with a good will.
biblical_def: Lief is the old English word for gladly — and behind the adverb stands an adjective meaning dear, for the root that gives us lief also gives us love and the -lief of belief. To do a thing lief is to do it because you hold it dear; the willingness and the love are one word. It does not appear in the Authorized Version, but the thing it names runs through Scripture under the word willing, and it is precisely what fallen men do not have and God alone can give. Of Christ’s subjects the Psalmist sings, “Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power” (Psa 110:3) — not conscripted but made lief; the power that works the willingness does not crush the will but frees it. That is effectual calling in half a verse. Of Christ Himself the word is perfect: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart” (Psa 40:8). He obeyed lief — not grudgingly, not of necessity laid on Him from outside, but gladly, because He loved the Father and the law was in His heart. And so the Christian’s giving is measured: “if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted” (2Co 8:12). When David’s people offered for the temple “with perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD” and the king rejoiced with great joy (1Ch 29:9). God has never wanted a service He had to drag out of us. He makes His people lief, and then delights in the gladness He Himself gave.
webster_summary: Dear, beloved; and as an adverb, gladly, willingly, with a good will — kin to love and belief.
webster_full: LIEF, a. Dear; beloved; held precious.
LIEF, adv. Gladly; willingly; with a good will — as in “I had as lief.”
From the Saxon lēof, “dear”; the same root as love and be-lief.
The willingness and the loving are one word: what is lief to a man he does gladly.
It is an English word, not a KJV word; Scripture names the thing willing.
scriptures: Psa 40:8
I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.
Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth.
Then the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD: and David the king also rejoiced with great joy.
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for glad willingness; it recovers that God does not conscript His people — He makes them willing in the day of His power.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a grudging religion. Half of what men render to God they render because they suppose they must, and the offering smells of the compulsion. Paul says the gift is accepted “if there be first a willing mind” — the mind before the money, the gladness before the gift. When David’s people brought their gold for the house of the LORD, the text will not let the point go: they offered willingly, and with perfect heart they offered willingly, and the king rejoiced with great joy. Duty done lief is worship; duty done grudgingly is a tax, and God has never been in want of revenue.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sovereign grace produces glad willingness, and does not violate it. Men imagine that if God works the will He must therefore break it — that grace and gladness are rivals, and that a man is only free when God has left him alone. Psalm 110:3 answers them: “Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power.” The power and the willingness arrive together. The Spirit does not drag the elect to Christ against their liking; He gives them a new liking, so that the man who would not come now would not stay away. And the pattern is the Son Himself, of whom it is written, “I delight to do thy will, O my God” — obedience rendered lief, because the law was in His heart.
roots_summary: The word means dear, and so gladly — kin to love and to the -lief of belief.
roots_lines: Lief — Old English lēof, “dear, beloved, pleasing.”
The same root gives love and the -lief of belief.
As an adjective it means dear; as an adverb, gladly, willingly.
It survives in the old phrase “I had as lief,” I would as gladly.
Scripture names the thing willing: made so in the day of His power (Psa 110:3).
usage: Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power — grace does not break the will, it frees it.
I delight to do thy will: Christ obeyed lief, because the law was already within His heart.
If there be first a willing mind it is accepted — the gladness before the gift, or it is a tax.
